Update on the Take Care of America’s Veterans Act

Requesting Unanimous Consent to Pass Landmark Veterans Legislation

This week, I went to the Senate floor to request unanimous consent (UC) to pass my legislation, the Take Care of America’s Veterans Act. This legislation is the single best path forward to meaningfully improve the lives of millions of veterans, survivors, families and caregivers and create a better, stronger and modernized VA to provide critical care to those who have served. Many veterans, survivors and caregivers have waited years for the reforms in this legislation to become law. They should not have to wait any longer, and as chairman of the Senate Committee on Veterans’ Affairs, I am committed to delivering real results for them as soon as possible.

While on the Senate floor, I also objected to a motion from my colleague and the Ranking Member of the Senate Committee on Veterans’ Affairs, Sen. Richard Blumenthal (D-Conn.) to attempt to pay for the Take Care of America’s Veterans Act by rescinding funds from the Department of Defense. The Congressional Budget Office has confirmed that this approach does not work. I continue to work hard to find a way to pass the Take Care of America’s Veterans Act swiftly.

More Than 20 Veterans Organizations Announce Support for the Legislation

Many organizations that support the Take Care of America’s Veterans Act have used their voices and platforms to advocate for Congress to pass this important legislation over the last two months. This week, more than 20 groups joined together in calling on Congress to pass the bill, stating: “Congress has an opportunity to do what is right by delivering meaningful support to those who served this nation in uniform, as well as the families, caregivers and survivors who carry the burden alongside them. We have heard their calls for help for decades. The Take Care of America’s Veterans Act is how those calls can be answered. The good this bill would do for the community is clear, and the time to act is now.”

This statement was sent by a number of veterans organizations, including The American Legion, the Military Officers Association of America, Wounded Warrior Project, the Elizabeth Dole Foundation, Tragedy Assistance Program for Survivors, American Veterans (AMVETS) and more. I thank them and all of the organizations that continue to support this monumental legislation that would benefit millions of veterans, families, caregivers, survivors and VA staff members, as we work to advance this legislation to the President’s desk. Read the coalition statement and find the full list of supporters here.

Receiving Briefing from Secretary Hegseth on Iran Conflict

The conflict with Iran remains tense as Iran continues to attack military installations hosting U.S. troops as well as shipping in the Strait of Hormuz. The United States has retaliated for the attacks and maintains a blockade on Iranian shipping in an effort to stop Iran’s oil exports. As President Trump has reportedly declined to expand attacks on Iran due to depleted critical munitions, I met with Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth on Wednesday night to discuss in a classified setting the extent to which Congress needs to make certain our forces have the capabilities they need to execute missions.

Meeting with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy

This week, I joined a bipartisan group of senators to meet with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy. During our discussion, we discussed the importance of increasing economic pressure on Russia through sanctions legislation I introduced with a bipartisan group of my colleagues, including the late Sen. Lindsey Graham. President Zelenskyy also provided an update on Ukraine's ongoing efforts to defend itself against Russia's unprovoked aggression.

The U.S. must continue to stand with Ukraine and our NATO allies while holding Vladimir Putin accountable for his continued assault on a sovereign nation. America is strongest when we lead with our values, stand by our allies and defend liberty at home and abroad.

Paying Tribute to Sen. Lindsey Graham

On Tuesday, Congress paused to honor the life and legacy of Sen. Lindsey Graham. He was an American patriot, and he cared deeply about promoting liberty and fighting tyranny throughout the world. Through my time serving with him in the United States Senate, his devotion to our country was evident. Sen. Graham was passionate in supporting America’s servicemembers, defending our nation’s interests and serving the state of South Carolina.

We worked together on efforts to bolster our national security and promote freedom around the globe. We also served as co-chairs of the Senate National Institutes of Health (NIH) Caucus, working to support federal investments in research to save lives and promote access to new treatments and care. His leadership in the United States Senate will be missed. Robba and I are thinking of his sister, Se. Darline Graham, his staff and all his loved ones in this difficult time.

Participating in Joint Air and Space Force Caucus Roundtable

This week, as co-chair of the Space Force Caucus, I joined several of my Senate colleagues for a discussion with senior leaders of the U.S. Air Force and U.S. Space Force, including Secretary of the Air Force Troy Meink, Chief of Staff of the Air Force Gen. Kenneth Wilsbach, Vice Chief of Space Operations Gen. Shawn Bratton, Chief Master Sergeant of the Air Force David Wolfe and Chief Master Sergeant of the Space Force John Bentivegna. As our adversaries invest heavily in capabilities designed to challenge American airpower and contest our access to space, these conversations are essential to make certain Congress provides our military with the resources it needs.

During the discussion, I highlighted Kansas’ critical role in our nation’s defense, including McConnell Air Force Base’s role as home to the KC-46A Pegasus tanker and the dedicated men and women of the 22nd Air Refueling Wing who support our Air Force to project power around the world. As the Air Capital of the World, Kansas has long been a leader in aviation, and our skilled manufacturing workforce and aerospace suppliers are now playing an increasingly important role in strengthening America’s growing space industrial base by building the components and technologies needed to maintain our leadership in space. I will continue working with Air Force and Space Force leadership to support our servicemembers, strengthen our capabilities and make certain Kansas remains at the forefront of our national defense.

Introducing Legislation to Help Survivors of Human Trafficking Flee Their Captors

This week, I introduced bipartisan legislation with Sen. Cortez Masto (D-Nev.) to help survivors of human trafficking access air travel and resources they need to reach safety. Victims of human trafficking often lack a government-issued ID needed for air travel, hindering their ability to find safety or reunite with family. The Jimmy Deal Trafficking Survivors Assistance Act would establish a partnership between Transportation Security Administration (TSA) agents and anti-human trafficking service providers to eliminate this barrier by creating a process that helps make certain every survivor has the means to access air travel when they desperately need it to escape danger and reach safety. I will continue to advocate for the needs of survivors in Kansas and across the country to make certain they receive the care and support they need. You can read more about the legislation here.

Meeting with FCC Chairman Brendan Carr

This week, I met with Chairman Brendan Carr of the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) to discuss an update on the FCC’s role in regulating interstate and international communications by radio, television, wire, satellite and cable in the U.S. As the federal agency responsible for implementing and enforcing America’s communications laws and regulations, the FCC plays a significant role in supporting access to reliable communications services across the nation.

During our meeting, we discussed the one-year anniversary of the FCC’s Build America Agenda, which has helped strengthen broadband deployment, advance U.S. leadership in wireless and space technologies, and bolster our nation’s security and economic growth. I emphasized the valuable role local broadcasters play in Kansas and the importance of preserving access to community journalism across our state. Through my role on the Senate Committee on Commerce, Science and Transportation, which oversees the FCC, I continue to make certain that the FCC pursues policies that benefit Kansans.

Meeting with Jeff and Grant Seibel of Hays

It was great to catch up with Hays natives, Jeff Seibel and his son, Grant, during their visit to Washington, D.C., on Wednesday. Jeff and I were classmates at the University of Kansas School of Law, and I appreciated talking with him about the latest updates in Hays, as well as hearing from him and Grant about their time in our nation’s capital. Thank you to Jeff and Grant for their time and conversation.

Visits Across Kansas

AVI Technical Academy in Delphos

On Friday, I visited the Automotive Video (AVI) Technical Academy in Delphos, where I met with AVI owner Paul Louwers to discuss the importance of technical education designed to fast-track the careers of entry-level technicians, trade school graduates and experienced mechanics. Opening its academy in Delphos in 2025, AVI combines intensive classroom instruction with hands-on shop experience to prepare the next generation of high-tech talent, and it was great to learn more about how AVI is providing Kansans with the skills and training needed to succeed in today’s workforce. By bringing classroom learning together with real-world experience, facilities like AVI help students and workers pursue rewarding careers while strengthening the skilled workforce needed by communities and industries across Kansas. AVI is also committed to investing in the community, planning to build a new restaurant and an early education center in Delphos.

Thank you to AVI owner Paul Louwers and his sister, Connie Brown, Kansas Senator Elaine Bower, State Representative Dawn Wolf, Delphos City Council Member Terry Greer and Ottawa County Commissioner Scott Mortimer for joining me during my visit.

Clay Center Community Visit

Later on Friday, I traveled to Clay Center to meet with members of the community and to join Kyle Bauer of KFRM Radio in studio for an interview on the latest updates from my visits across Kansas. We also discussed the latest on the Farm Bill, as well as my efforts to pass the Major Richard Star Act and several other key bills included in the Take Care of America’s Veterans Act. You can listen to our conversation here.

During my visit, I stopped at Prairie Land Partners, Grow Clay County, Mayo Clothing and the Clay County Law Enforcement Center where I met with Clay County Sheriff Alan Benninga. I also spoke with Kansans at the U.S. Department of Agriculture Service Center, the local Pizza Hut, City Hall and the Clay County Courthouse, where I met with the Clay County Clerk Kayla Wang, County Register of Deeds Susan Mall and County Clerk of the Court Melissa Stellner.

I also visited Clay County Medical Center and met with CEO Austin Gillard.

Happy 90th Birthday Sen. Elizabeth Dole

This week marked the 90th birthday of my dear friend and honorary Kansan, Sen. Elizabeth Dole! I’m grateful for all she has done and continues to do for our nation’s veterans and their caregivers through the Dole Foundation, and I appreciate our years of friendship.

Honoring Former Kansas State Rep. Don Myers

I was saddened to learn of the passing of Don Myers of Derby, someone who was loved and respected by his community. As a former Kansas state representative and a United States Navy veteran, Don dedicated his life to serving Kansas, his community and his country. He was devoted to his wife, Mary, their family and their church, and his life embodied the meaning of public service. He and Mary valued giving back to others, and their faith was especially important to them. Robba and I are thinking of his family and loved ones during this difficult time. Don will be missed, and he will be remembered for the difference he made in the lives of so many.

Marking 68 Years of NASA & Kansans’ Contributions in Space Exploration

On July 29th, 1958, President Dwight D. Eisenhower signed the National Aeronautics and Space Act, establishing NASA and launching America into the race to the Moon. From President Eisenhower’s leadership to Clyde Tombaugh’s historic discovery of Pluto and Belleville native Nick Hague’s service aboard the International Space Station, Kansans continue to play a meaningful role in our nation’s space program.

68 years after NASA’s founding, the United States remains at the forefront of a new era of space exploration through the Artemis program. Across Kansas, manufacturers, engineers, scientists and technicians continue to support this mission and help advance American leadership in discovery and innovation.

text:
ROLLS-ROYCE SAYS NEW AIRBUS A350-2000 WOULD REQUIRE AN ALL-NEW ENGINE

Rolls-Royce says a larger Airbus A350, widely known as the A350-2000, would require a completely new engine program lasting six to seven years. If Airbus launches the aircraft around 2027, entry into service could come by 2033 or 2034.

Rather than an upgraded Trent XWB, the aircraft would rely on Rolls-Royce’s next-generation UltraFan technology, designed to deliver 10%–25% better fuel efficiency while operating on 100% Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF).

The company says it is taking a cautious approach, aiming to avoid the reliability and financial challenges experienced during the Trent 1000 program. Airbus has yet to approve the project but continues to study demand for a larger twin-engine aircraft capable of replacing aging Airbus A380s.

If launched, the stretched A350 would compete directly with Boeing’s 777-9 and could become a leading replacement for high-capacity aircraft. Emirates is widely viewed as a potential launch customer, thanks to its massive A380 fleet and long-standing interest in larger airliners.

Before the program moves forward, Airbus must determine whether market demand justifies the investment, while Rolls-Royce will need to develop and certify the new engine that would power the aircraft.

text:
Global stock markets faced volatility in July due to a number of factors, among them:

Renewed hostilities between the United States and Iran following the end of the ceasefire;

Rising oil prices, fuelling renewed concerns about inflation and the increased likelihood of a US interest rate increase in September;

Selling pressure on technology and artificial intelligence (AI) stocks due to concerns that higher costs will impact earnings;

The US announcing new tariffs on 60 countries.

Even the release of second-quarter earnings reports by listed companies, while mostly better than expected, could not offset the aforementioned risks.

In the Middle East, President Donald Trump warned that if the Iran-backed Houthi rebels attack ships in the Bab al-Mandeb Strait again, the US would retaliate with a heavy offensive against Iran and the Houthis.

He is seriously considering a return to large-scale military operations against Iran, potentially including attacks more severe than "Epic Fury", the joint US-Israeli campaign that began in late February. However, Trump said he has not made a final decision on the matter.

On the trade front, a new round of tariffs has been announced on imports from 60 countries, at rates between 10% and 12.5%. Thailand is subject to the 12.5% rate. Washington claims it enforced the levies because the countries have not done enough to combat forced labour, either in their domestic markets or in countries that supply materials used in their exports, which creates an unfair competitive advantage.

We believe the impact of the new tariffs is minimal as they simply replace the previous 10% global import tariff under Section 122 of the 1974 Trade Act, which was a temporary fix after the US Supreme Court ruled earlier that Trump's "reciprocal" tariffs were unconstitutional.

We expect factors influencing asset prices this month to include the following:

Whether tensions in the Middle East will ease. If negotiations resume, it would lower oil prices and reduce inflation concerns, positively impacting global stock markets;

The Federal Reserve's interest rate hike outlook;

Second-quarter earnings. Positive earnings and better-than-expected future profit outlooks would provide significant support. We recommend gradually accumulating shares in the US, Chinese and Vietnamese stock markets, while we continue to recommend accumulating gold at a price level of $4,000 an ounce.

AUGUST OUTLOOK

In August, the SET index is expected to find continued support from a stabilising macroeconomic backdrop, characterised by easing inflation concerns and expectations that ongoing geopolitical conflicts are unlikely to escalate significantly.

This more favourable external environment is driving a strategic fund flow rotation into domestic economy-linked equities and low-volatility stocks, as investors increasingly reallocate capital away from highly volatile, tech-exposed assets.

Despite this defensive anchor, market fluctuations are expected to heighten as the second-quarter earnings season winds down. Consequently, we place significant weight on adopting a highly selective investment strategy during this reporting period.

Individual corporate results will likely trigger substantial sector rotation, necessitating a strict stock-picking focus on companies demonstrating robust, visible earnings delivery to effectively navigate the market. Our picks for August are Bangchak Corporation (BCP), True Corporation (TRUE) and Bumrungrad Hospital (BH).

BCP (target price 61 baht): Earnings are expected to grow steadily from 2026–29, supported by a strong gross refining margin, contributions from the sustainable aviation fuel business, and profit recognition from the Hong Kong oil retail business starting in the third quarter of 2026. Meanwhile, the impact of lower oil prices is expected to be limited, given the relatively small earnings contribution from the exploration and production business. The stock remains a laggard among refinery peers, trading at just 0.6 times price/book value and 6 times price/earnings. We also expect solid earnings in the second and third quarters, with potential upside from the reinstatement of the share buyback programme.

TRUE (target 16 baht): Second quarter-core profit is projected to rise 56% year-on-year and 1% on the quarter, driven by continued growth in mobile and fixed broadband revenue, alongside lower network costs, spectrum expenses and interest costs. For full-year 2026, earnings are expected to grow 35%, significantly outpacing the projected 12% for ADVANC, while the stock continues to trade at a more attractive valuation than its peer.

title: Senate Farm Bill includes E15, SRE reforms | Ethanol Producer Magazine
description:
The newly released Farm Bill draft, formally titled the Agricultural Act of 2026, builds on the Farm Bill 2.0 discussion draft released by the committee in June.
The committee, however, has added a new subtitle to the Farm Bill 2.0 draft that provides for year-round E15 and implements reforms to the RFS’s SRE program.
In conjunction with the E15 language, the legislation also includes provisions that would significantly alter the RFS SRE program starting in 2028.
Once the Senate approves its bill, a conference committee will likely be formed to merge the House and Senate legislation into one final version of the 2026 Farm Bill.
Additional information, including a full copy of the Senate’s updated Farm Bill draft, is available on the Senate Agriculture Committee website.
text:
The U.S. Senate Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition and Forestry on July 31 released an updated draft of its 2026 Farm Bill 2.0 that includes language to enable year-round sales of E15 and revamp the Renewable Fuel Standard small refinery exemption (SRE) program. The bill’s Energy Title also contains numerous provisions supporting sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) and other biobased fuels.

The newly released Farm Bill draft, formally titled the Agricultural Act of 2026, builds on the Farm Bill 2.0 discussion draft released by the committee in June. No major changes were made to the legislation’s Energy Title, which still includes a major revamp of the USDA’s Section 9003 loan guarantee program, including language allowing grants of up to $10 million for certain eligible projects.

The committee, however, has added a new subtitle to the Farm Bill 2.0 draft that provides for year-round E15 and implements reforms to the RFS’s SRE program.

For E15, the bill aims to permanently authorize nationwide year-round sales of E15, expanding consumer fuel choice, strengthening domestic biofuels, and providing long-term regulatory certainty.

In conjunction with the E15 language, the legislation also includes provisions that would significantly alter the RFS SRE program starting in 2028. Petitions filed under the current SRE program would not be accepted after July 1, 2028, and the bill would require the U.S. EPA to act on all outstanding SRE petitions by Oct. 1, 2028.

Beginning in 2028, the EPA would reduce the annual renewable volume obligation (RVO) for eligible small refineries by a volume equal to the lesser of 1) the greatest actual annual production volume of transportation fuel by the small refinery during any of calendar years 2023-2025 for which the refinery filed an SRE petition by June 1, 2026, and met the requirements, or 2) the actual annual production volume of transportation fuel produced by the small refinery during the calendar year during which the EPA is applying the reduction. The legislation also includes provisions reallocating waived volumes in excess of 500 million gallons.

In addition to the E15 and SRE provisions, the Senate Farm Bill renames the Section 9003 Biorefinery, Renewable Chemical Biobased Product Manufacturing Program as the Biorefinery, Renewable Chemical, Biobased Products Manufacturing and Sustainable Aviation Fuel Assistance Program. The bill also updates the purpose of the program from one exclusively focused on the development of new and emerging technologies to one focused both on the development of new and emerging technologies and the development of projects to produce advanced biofuels, renewable chemicals, biobased products and SAF.

As part of the change, the scope of the 9003 program is expanded to include support for both technologically new and innovative commercial-scale projects. The Farm Bill 2.0 draft also allows the USDA to waive the feasibility study currently required by the 9003 program for proven or otherwise commercially available technologies.

Other updates to the 9003 program include those that aim to streamline the application process and allow for grants of up to $10 million to support the development, construction or retrofitting of biorefineries for converting renewable biomass to biofuels, renewable chemicals, SAF and biobased products.

The Senate’s Farm Bill 2.0 would also updated the USDA’s Rural Energy for America Program by authorizing grants to organizations that provide technical assistance for agriculture producers and rural small businesses applying for REAP funds; establishing a rebate pilot project for purchases of certain energy efficient equipment incurred outside the application period; increasing eligible project size from $25 million to $50 million; and directing the USDA to provide a simplified application process for projects less than $50,000 .

Other provisions of the bill expand and strengthen the BioPreferred Program and strengthen reporting of biobased products that are purchased through online federal procurement systems, including use of North American Industry Classification System (NAICS) codes.

The Senate’s Farm Bill would clarify SAF qualifies as an advanced biofuel and direct the USDA to establish an agency-wide strategy to advance the production of SAF. In addition, Farm Bill 2.0 would extend the authorization of appropriations for the Bioenergy Program for Advanced Biofuels, Biodiesel Fuel Education Program, Feedstock Flexibility Program for Bioenergy Producers, the Biomass Crop Assistance Program, and the Carbon Utilization and Biogas Education Program through 2031.

The U.S. House of Representatives passed its version of the 2026 Farm Bill on April 30. The Energy Title of that legislation shares some similarities with the Senate’s Farm Bill 2.0, including provisions related to qualifying SAF as an advanced biofuel and encouraging USDA to develop a strategy to expand to the production of SAF.

The Senate Agriculture Committee is scheduled to begin the markup process on Aug. 6. After the committee approves the bill, it can be brought to vote in the full Senate. Once the Senate approves its bill, a conference committee will likely be formed to merge the House and Senate legislation into one final version of the 2026 Farm Bill. That compromised legislative package will need to be approved by both the House and Senate before it can be submitted to President Trump for his consideration.

Additional information, including a full copy of the Senate’s updated Farm Bill draft, is available on the Senate Agriculture Committee website.

text:
Valero Energy Corp. released second quarter financial results on July 30, reporting significantly improved earnings for both its ethanol segment and its Diamond Green Diesel joint venture, which produces renewable diesel and sustainable aviation fuel (SAF).

The ethanol segment reported $318 million of operating income for the second quarter of 2026, up from $64 million during the same period of last year. Valero’s 12 ethanol plants produced 4.67 million gallons per day of ethanol during the three-month period, up from 4.58 million gallons per day during the second quarter of 2025. Ethanol margin per gallon of production was $1.15, up from 52 cents. Operating income was 75 per gallon, up from 13 cents per gallon.

The renewable diesel segment, which consists of the DGD joint venture, reported $717 million in operating income for the second quarter, compared to an operating loss of $79 million reported for the same period of 2025. Segment operating volumes averaged 3.83 million gallons per day, up from 2.73 million gallons per day during the same period of last year.

During a second quarter earnings call, Calero Chief Financial Officer Homer Bhullar said the company expects sales volumes for the renewable diesel segment to reach approximately 335 million gallons in the third quarter, with ethanol production at 4.8 million gallons per day.

Bhullar also noted Valero is pursuing projects to increase efficiency and production at some of its ethanol plants. Eric Honeyman, senior vice president of renewables operations and low carbon fuels, noted the company is looking at small debottleneck projects to the extent of 100 to 200 million gallons per year. Those projects are currently expected to be online in the next year or two.

Honeyman also noted Valero’s ethanol operations are benefiting from the 45Z clean fuel production credit. He estimated the credit has been 14 cents per gallon year to date and will probably grow to 17 cents per gallon for the full year, with a credit of approximately 19 cents per gallon expected for 2027-2029.

title: Air Canada, Airbus launch €9.2 million initiative to boost SAF production in Canada
description:
Air Canada and Airbus have announced plans to establish a jointly funded Sustainability Co-Investment Platform to accelerate the development of a commercial-scale Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF) industry in Canada.
The two companies will invest up to €9.2 million to support SAF innovation and production, with the aim of helping advance a Canadian SAF project to a Final Investment Decision (FID), biofuels international reported.
The partners said the initiative is intended to stimulate domestic SAF production by leveraging Canada’s abundant feedstock resources while supporting the aviation sector’s decarbonisation goals.
A key objective of the platform is to identify and support a jointly selected Canadian SAF project capable of progressing to commercial deployment.
Air Canada said the initiative will also help corporate customers reduce emissions associated with business travel by expanding access to sustainable aviation fuel.
text:
Air Canada and Airbus have announced plans to establish a jointly funded Sustainability Co-Investment Platform to accelerate the development of a commercial-scale Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF) industry in Canada.

The two companies will invest up to €9.2 million to support SAF innovation and production, with the aim of helping advance a Canadian SAF project to a Final Investment Decision (FID), biofuels international reported.

The partners said the initiative is intended to stimulate domestic SAF production by leveraging Canada’s abundant feedstock resources while supporting the aviation sector’s decarbonisation goals. They added that a supportive public policy framework will be essential to scale up production and attract further investment.

A key objective of the platform is to identify and support a jointly selected Canadian SAF project capable of progressing to commercial deployment.

Air Canada and Airbus said they will continue working with federal and provincial governments, as well as the Canadian Council for Sustainable Aviation Fuels (C-SAF), to develop policies that encourage large-scale SAF production and improve the availability and affordability of renewable aviation fuels.

Air Canada said the initiative will also help corporate customers reduce emissions associated with business travel by expanding access to sustainable aviation fuel.

Airbus said long-term collaboration across the aviation industry will be critical to decarbonising air transport, noting that sustained investment in renewable energy and low-carbon fuels will be needed over the coming decades.

title: Ascension Parish ends mitigation efforts at LAlumina site as permanent closure phase begins
description:
The former LAlumina site in Ascension Parish has transitioned to long-term closure under LDEQ oversight, according to Ascension Business Report.
Ascension Parish began temporary mitigation efforts in 2024 after years of complaints from nearby residents about red bauxite residue, or “red dust,” blowing from uncovered waste ponds onto homes, vehicles and other property.
During the project, parish crews covered more than 40 acres across Ponds 4 and 5 with soil to suppress dust, reduce erosion and encourage vegetation growth while a permanent closure plan was finalized.
Permanent site remediation is expected to cost between $13 million and $18 million.
The project will use the remaining $5 million in a trust fund established by LAlumina, with the company responsible for the remaining costs.
text:
The former LAlumina site in Ascension Parish has transitioned to long-term closure under LDEQ oversight, according to Ascension Business Report.

Ascension Parish began temporary mitigation efforts in 2024 after years of complaints from nearby residents about red bauxite residue, or “red dust,” blowing from uncovered waste ponds onto homes, vehicles and other property. During the project, parish crews covered more than 40 acres across Ponds 4 and 5 with soil to suppress dust, reduce erosion and encourage vegetation growth while a permanent closure plan was finalized.

Although the parish’s formal role has ended, it will continue supplying soil from drainage maintenance projects as needed.

The former alumina refinery, originally built in the late 1950s, closed in 2020. Permanent site remediation is expected to cost between $13 million and $18 million. The project will use the remaining $5 million in a trust fund established by LAlumina, with the company responsible for the remaining costs.

text:
Sustainable aviation fuel could increase corn demand by billions of bushels annually.

Ethanol blended with gasoline for on-road vehicles has played a huge part in shaping the corn industry for the last two decades. Just this year, ethanol production used 4.42 billion bushels and accounted for 27.2% of total corn demand. As corn farmers continue to produce more on their acres, new sources of demand are needed to match the growing supply. One of those new sources of demand the National Corn Growers Association is pursuing is sustainable aviation fuel (SAF). American corn, processed into ethanol can help airplanes take to the skies.

Why does sustainable aviation fuel matter?

Sustainable aviation fuel opens a world of opportunity to increase corn demand. It would take 1.7 billion bushels of corn to fuel just 10% of global aviation needs. The aviation sector continues to prioritize greenhouse gas emission reduction. And it’s not just airlines. Fuel producers, commercial customers, and governments are also rapidly searching for solutions. They need something scalable, commercially viable, and low-carbon – all of which SAF can provide. It’s a win-win: low-carbon fuel for aviation and more corn demand for U.S. farmers.

Why is ethanol a good fit for SAF?

U.S. corn-based ethanol already has the pieces in place to support large-scale SAF production. From corn supply to production capacity, it is one of the most immediate and abundant domestic feedstocks on the market. And beyond production readiness, using homegrown fuel strengthens American energy security while creating substantial new demand for U.S. corn growers.

"As we see a steady decline in on-road consumption of ethanol, we need to continually look for new ways to utilize corn,” said Sean Arians, vice president of sustainable production & value chain engagement at NCGA. “SAF provides a pathway for consumption of ethanol in the alcohol to jet pathway."

How is federal policy helping to produce SAF?

The Clean Fuel Production Tax Credit (45z) incentivizes ethanol manufacturers to produce SAF. The tax credit helps farmers make inroads into the aviation sector. Stable, long-term market incentives for ethanol producers provide farmers the chance to access reliable markets. This allows farmers to make capital, input, and management decisions that set up their operations to supply the SAF market for years to come while also adding certainty to their operation’s future.

What still needs to happen?

NCGA is working to position U.S. corn up as the premier feedstock for SAF, including accurate accounting for life cycle/carbon intensity modeling, overcoming misconceptions about food supply vs. corn for feed, and evolving U.S. and international regulatory and policy strategy.

Like other industries, such as maritime fuels, the frameworks most often used to account for carbon intensity do not fully recognize the vast improvements farmers have made in sustainability and efficiency in recent decades. To change this, NCGA continues to advocate for federal SAF implementation guidance that properly accounts for improvements in corn production efficiencies on farms today, leveling the playing field for U.S. corn growers.

When looking at solutions surrounding U.S. and global regulatory processes and policy, NCGA is focused on favorable SAF investment policies, engagement in the International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO), and mandates from the European Union.

Favorable SAF investment policies like 45Z are a great start. NCGA supports policy and market-based incentives to lower the cost of finished fuel, encouraging airline uptake.

Engagement in ICAO aims to ensure U.S. corn is an eligible feedstock for SAF. NCGA is calling for stronger engagement from the administration, including the United States Department of Agriculture, Department of Energy, Environmental Protection Agency, the Federal Aviation Administration and the State Department to ensure U.S. interests are represented.

European Union SAF mandates will continue to heavily influence the SAF market. The current mandate does not allow for U.S. crop-based biofuels to be used in SAF. NCGA is working with U.S. policymakers to avoid discriminatory treatment of U.S. ethanol.

Bottom Line

“In order to grow demand, we must identify new opportunities. One promising market is sustainable aviation fuel,” said Illinois farmer and NCGA Biofuels Action Team Chair Jon Rosenstiel. "Advocating for SAF now will help the future of corn farming beyond my generation, but we must start now in order for this demand to grow."

text:
A substantial inventory of unused equipment and materials from a canceled large-scale renewable fuels project is now available for purchase through AllSurplus on behalf of Shell, creating a unique opportunity for companies involved in renewable fuels, refining, chemical processing and other industrial sectors to acquire high-value, never-used assets.

The equipment originates from a renewable diesel and sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) facility that was under development before the project was canceled. The planned facility included process units for feedstock pretreatment, hydrogen manufacturing, renewable diesel and SAF production, biogas treatment and supporting storage infrastructure.

The sale includes a wide range of unused process equipment, rotating machinery, pressure vessels, electrical equipment, construction materials and balance-of-plant assets that can support new facility construction, plant expansions, maintenance projects or equipment replacements.

Specialized process equipment is being offered through a "make an offer" sale format, while commodity-type assets and construction materials will be sold in a series of online auctions, providing buyers with multiple opportunities to acquire equipment that is immediately available.

The inventory represents a rare opportunity for project developers, engineering firms, equipment suppliers and plant operators seeking to reduce procurement timelines and capital costs. With continued investment in renewable fuels, sustainable aviation fuel and other industrial decarbonization projects around the world, demand remains strong for high-quality process equipment that can be deployed without the lead times associated with new manufacturing.

In addition to major process equipment, the sale includes a broad selection of construction materials and supporting infrastructure components suitable for a variety of industrial applications. These assets can be repurposed for renewable fuels, refining, chemical manufacturing and other process industries.

title: Retail aviation fuel saw slight relief through July, though high prices persist overall
description:

text:
Who doesn't love a game of red light, green light?

Well, it's a bit less fun when it takes place Squid Game-style in the Strait of Hormuz. The memorandum of understanding (MOU) between the United States and Iran deteriorated almost immediately, though not before delivering a brief respite from the elevated prices that all points in the supply chain have been absorbing for months. At present, the situation is reliant on knee-jerk fluctuations caused by diplomatic conversations (or less-diplomatic destruction).

On the surface, the U.S. and Iran continue to trade fire. Iran remains determined to enforce passage fees through the strait, and the U.S. still disagrees. Opposed to Iran's control of the strait, Oman has proposed a Gulf-backed compromise modeled after the Strait of Malacca's voluntary fee structure. Under this framework, ships would be asked to contribute to navigation and safety operations, and Iran would not have sole administrative control. Don't get your hopes up – the U.S. has already rejected this, reiterating that the strait is an international waterway that should remain free of fees or single-state management. The core dispute remains unresolved.

Is the strait open? Technically yes, but you'll be wading through an active warzone with a target on your back. Maritime intelligence firm Windward rates the strait's operational risk as critical, with the strait effectively closed to routine commercial shipping. Windward data counted 20 ships that crossed the strait on July 29 (10 in, 10 out), with 5 of those ships operating dark by shutting down transponders and lights. U.S. Energy Secretary Chris Wright has stated that American military escorts are helping oil and gas tankers move through the strait.

Compounding this issue, the Houthis – an Iran-aligned militant group based in Yemen – have declared a blockade of Saudi Red Sea ports on July 20, causing ships to reroute in response. With both the Strait of Hormuz and the Red Sea now disrupted, there is no clean route out of the Gulf. This is not an ideal situation for global energy and trade markets.

100LL AvGas

Strictly looking at national averages month over month, 100LL appears to have plateaued. Averaging $7.46 in June, the national average for 100LL has dropped just one cent in July to $7.45.

As is often the case, a granular analysis tells a far less linear story. The wholesale dip that followed the MOU ceasefire pushed prices down significantly at the start of July. However, that relief is already being reversed. Current 100LL rates are already higher than they were 30 days ago (with the exception of Alaska decreasing by 18 cents and the Northwest Mountain staying constant). Sorry, New England – you boast the largest 100LL increase in that timeframe at 11 cents.

Moral of the story? Time your resupply after a strategic 'diplomatic conversation' in the Middle East. I have a feeling we'll be getting friendly with these sporadic respites for a while yet.

Jet A

Jet A offered some relief through July as well, with the national average dropping from $7.74 to $7.52. That said, similar to 100LL, Jet A is once again on the upswing.

Without exception, Jet A has risen over the past 30 days in every single FAA region. The average increase was 27 cents, with a standard deviation of 13 cents. For context, the highest recorded monthly national average GlobalAir.com recorded prior to 2026 for Jet A was $7.25 in July 2022. Even accounting for inflation, this crisis has sustained aviation retail prices at unprecedented levels – a point explored in Abby's Ramp Ramble – Fuel Price Crisis.

The Jet A trade is considerably more complex than 100LL given both its scale and role across corporate and commercial aviation. These operators are often more diversified in their ability to absorb elevated rates. However, Spirit Airlines is proof that even more elastic organizations have their limits, citing the fuel price spike as a final blow toward full shutdown.

Sustainable Aviation Fuel

Making almost too much sense, SAF continues to mirror Jet A, dropping from a national average of $9.76 for June to $9.57 for July, offering operators utilizing retail SAF similar relief at the pump.

In line with the trends we've seen in 100LL and Jet A, SAF has increased over the last 30 days for every FAA region with enough FBO reports to form a substantial average (New England, Eastern, Southern, Great Lakes, Southwest, Northwest Mountain and Western Pacific).

Ironically, this crisis makes the case for shifting to SAF stronger while simultaneously exposing the current supply chain's inefficiencies. Primarily derived from cooking oil and animal fats, pure SAF saw price increases not driven by crude oil disruptions, but by competition for feedstock. As conventional prices surged, biofuel industries increased feedstock demand to serve road transport markets seeking cheaper alternatives. A fully established SAF network wouldn't have prevented the Hormuz crisis, but a wider network could have meaningfully reduced aviation's exposure to it.

Most FBO managers will care little about SAF until they see actionable steps regarding regulation or demand. In fact, most FBOs providing SAF are selling a blended product rather than pure SAF, making retail prices more subject to crude disruptions. The prices posted by FBOs on GlobalAir.com reflect that mixture, which along with wholesale differentials, also explains why SAF follows Jet A so closely in our dataset.

The Big Picture

The situation remains unstable. Wholesale fluctuations have been sporadic and significant, but the situation at large is keeping margins thin. Negotiations continue to fall through and bombs continue to drop.

After a dip following the brief U.S.-Iran MOU, average fuel prices by FAA region jumped right back up, though measures to get crude oil through the strait could offer another supply boon at any moment.

Is the end in sight? Ask again later.

Top Performing Airports

It is no surprise that Wittman Regional (KOSH) ended up in our top airport list through July. Through the annual GlobalAir.com Oshkosh Specials Page, we were able to route thousands of transient pilots to over 130 FBOs offering unique fuel discounts or special offerings.

Pilots and flight departments use the GlobalAir.com Airport Resource Center to quickly research the entirety of their trip. From FBO fuel and services, pilot information, hotels and rentals, restaurants, airport businesses and everything in between, aviation professionals can access and review the best options all in one place.

Salt Lake City International Airport (KSLC) in Salt Lake City, UT

Top Performing FBOs

Despite a turbulent fuel market and the Oshkosh flight rush, these FBOs were able to maintain a strong foothold through July.

Big news for number one: JAX Executive Jet Center and Sky Harbor at KCRG have consolidated into Sky Harbor North and Sky Harbor South. Operations have not halted, so be sure to fly in next time you get a chance!

text:
Commission Approves €290 Million Dutch State Aid to Support Sustainable Aviation Fuels

(European Commission) The European Commission has approved, under EU State aid rules, two Dutch schemes with a combined budget of €290 million to support sustainable aviation fuels ('SAF'). The schemes will contribute to the objectives of the Clean Industrial Deal to accelerate the decarbonisation of EU industry, as well as of the ReFuelEU Aviation Regulation to boost the supply and demand of SAF and accelerate the transition to climate-neutral aviation.

The Dutch schemes

The Netherlands notified the Commission of its intention to introduce two schemes to support projects that produce SAF at different stages of their development. Although the schemes share a common budget, one provides investment aid for SAF production, while the other covers the costs of preparatory works for SAF projects including front-end engineering design studies. The approved schemes will support projects estimated to produce around 285 kilotonnes of SAF per year, the equivalent of 350 million litres of kerosene, or around 3,500 intercontinental flights.

The aid will be awarded on a first-come-first-served basis through schemes that are objective, non-discriminatory and transparent.

The schemes will provide support to two promising technology pathways: advanced bio-SAF not produced through the Hydroprocessed Esters and Fatty Acids process ('non-HEFA advanced bio-SAF'), and synthetic aviation fuels ('e-SAF'). The Netherlands believes that supporting these two types of SAF now will assist their commercial development, fostering technological diversity in the future.

Under the schemes, the aid will take the form of direct grants payable upon the completion of project milestones. The schemes will cover the period from 2027 until 2031 at the latest. Up to five rounds of funding will take place during this period, depending on the available funding. Beneficiaries of the scheme dedicated to support SAF production will have to prove compliance with the EU criteria for the production of renewable fuels of non-biological origin (RFNBOs) or the EU sustainability criteria for advanced biofuels.

The Commission's assessment

The Commission assessed the schemes under EU State aid rules, in particular Article 107(3)(c) of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union (TFEU), which enables Member States to support the development of certain economic activities under certain conditions, the 2022 Guidelines on State aid for climate, environmental protection and energy ('CEEAG'), and the 2025 Clean Industrial Deal State aid Framework ('CISAF').

In particular, the Commission found that:

The schemes are necessary and appropriate to facilitate the production of SAF;

The schemes have an incentive effect, as the beneficiaries would not carry out the relevant studies and investments without the public support;

The Netherlands put in place sufficient safeguards to ensure that the schemes have a limited impact on competition and trade within the EU;

Proportionality will be ensured through the application of the aid intensities applicable to the eligible costs that are set out in the relevant sections of the CISAF and CEEAG;

The aid will bring about positive effects, in particular on the environment, contributing to the Clean Industrial Deal objectives;

On this basis, the Commission approved the Dutch schemes under EU State aid rules.

Background

The 2025 Clean Industrial Deal State Aid Framework is the European Commission's temporary state aid rulebook designed to let Member States support investment in clean energy, industrial decarbonisation and clean technology manufacturing more quickly while safeguarding fair competition in the Single Market.

The Commission's 2022 CEEAG provide guidance on how the Commission assesses the compatibility of environmental protection, including climate protection, and energy aid measures which are subject to the notification requirement under Article 107(3)(c) TFEU.

The Renewable Energy Directive of 2018 set out stringent criteria for advanced biofuels, such as advanced bio-SAF, and renewable fuels of non-biological origin, such as e-SAF. These rules ensure that their environmental impact is minimal, including by requiring the greenhouse gas emission savings of end products to exceed certain thresholds across the entire value chain.

title: Why The Airbus A380 Is Having An Unexpected 2nd Life - Simple Flying
authors: Josh Eyre, Jacob Johnson, Abid Habib
description:
When the final Airbus A380 was handed over to Emirates in December 2021, it marked the end of one of the most ambitious commercial aircraft programs ever undertaken.
Instead of retiring aircraft, airlines have concluded that investing in heavy maintenance and cabin refurbishments is a better financial decision.
During the pandemic, the airline placed its A380 fleet into long-term storage in Spain and publicly indicated that the aircraft's commercial career with the carrier had effectively ended.
It never fulfilled Airbus' ambition of becoming the dominant aircraft connecting the world's largest hubs, nor will production ever restart.
Today, the superjumbo occupies a profitable niche that no other passenger aircraft can fully replicate, combining unmatched capacity with a premium passenger experience.
text:
When the final Airbus A380 was handed over to Emirates in December 2021, it marked the end of one of the most ambitious commercial aircraft programs ever undertaken. Originally launched with the expectation that airlines would increasingly funnel passengers through mega-hubs using ultra-large aircraft, the A380 instead entered a market that gradually shifted in the opposite direction.

Advances in twin-engine technology have enabled aircraft such as the Boeing 787 Dreamliner to connect smaller cities directly, reducing reliance on the traditional hub-and-spoke model. With only 251 aircraft built, far fewer than Airbus had originally anticipated, the program was brought to a close after nearly two decades. Almost five years later, the A380 has become one of aviation's most surprising success stories.

Around 190 aircraft remain in commercial service, representing roughly three-quarters of the entire fleet ever produced, while airlines continue to invest in refurbishment programs rather than accelerating retirements. Rather than being remembered as an aircraft overtaken by technology, the A380 has found a highly profitable niche.

This has been thanks to a combination of delayed aircraft deliveries, increasing airport congestion, record international travel demand and a renewed focus on premium passenger experience. Although no additional aircraft will ever be built, the world's largest passenger airliner is proving far more valuable in 2026 than many expected when production ceased.

The Aircraft Shortage Nobody Expected

In 2019, when Airbus announced it was ending production, airlines expected the aircraft to be gradually replaced by a new generation of efficient widebodies. The Boeing 777X was intended to become the flagship of many long-haul fleets, while Airbus continued expanding production of the A350 family and Boeing increased deliveries of the 787 Dreamliner.

Fleet planners typically make decisions many years in advance, carefully aligning aircraft deliveries with the retirement of older models to avoid unnecessary maintenance costs and maximize fuel efficiency. The reality facing airlines today is very different. The 777X program remains years behind its original entry-into-service target, delaying replacement plans for numerous carriers. At the same time, Airbus and Boeing both continue to work through historically large order backlogs.

Airbus has more than 9,000 commercial jets on its order books, while Boeing's backlog exceeds 6,000 jets across its commercial portfolio. Although production rates are increasing, manufacturers continue to face shortages of critical components, including engines, castings, avionics and cabin interiors. This has altered the economics of operating older fleets. Instead of retiring aircraft, airlines have concluded that investing in heavy maintenance and cabin refurbishments is a better financial decision.

Lufthansa illustrates this perfectly. During the pandemic, the airline placed its A380 fleet into long-term storage in Spain and publicly indicated that the aircraft's commercial career with the carrier had effectively ended. Today, Lufthansa is not only flying the A380 again but also investing in new business class cabins for the fleet.

No Aircraft Moves More Passengers Through One Airport Slot

Even if aircraft manufacturers could suddenly deliver hundreds of additional widebodies, airlines would still face another challenge that has become increasingly significant over the past decade: airport capacity. Some of the world's largest international hubs are effectively full for much of the day, leaving airlines with few opportunities to add extra flights even when passenger demand continues to grow. This environment plays directly into the A380's greatest strength.

Depending on the airline's configuration, the aircraft typically accommodates between 450 and 520 passengers, although Emirates' highest-density examples seat as many as 615 passengers. With that being said, the capacity of these types is being reduced in retrofits. By comparison, a 777-300ER generally carries around 350 to 390 passengers, while most A350-1000s seat between 350 and 410.

Although newer aircraft offer substantially lower fuel burn per flight, they cannot match the passenger volume an A380 can transport during a single airport movement. Where slots are scarce, airlines are often more concerned with maximizing passengers per departure than minimizing operating costs per aircraft. On routes where flights regularly depart full, adding another 100 to 200 seats without requiring another slot can generate significantly greater revenue than operating a smaller aircraft more efficiently.

Premium Demand Has Transformed The Business Case

Although economy class continues to account for the majority of passengers, an increasing proportion of airline profits now comes from premium cabins, with business class, first class and premium economy generating disproportionately high yields. In its latest Global Market Forecast, Airbus highlights a strong shift toward 'premiumization,' with high-end cabin seating expected to expand at a faster rate than overall passenger volume over the next two decades.

Its enormous cabin gives airlines a level of flexibility that simply does not exist on smaller aircraft. With two full-length passenger decks and around 5,920 square feet (550 square meters) of floor space, the A380 allows operators to dedicate substantially more room to premium products without dramatically reducing overall seating capacity.

Etihad's fleet became famous for introducing 'The Residence', a three-room private suite featuring a bedroom, lounge and ensuite shower. Passenger perception also continues to work in the A380's favor. The upper deck offers a noticeably quieter cabin than most twin-engine aircraft thanks to the distance from the engines, while the aircraft's immense fuselage creates a greater sense of space, particularly in premium cabins.

Airlines have capitalized on that reputation by marketing the A380 as a flagship. Choosing a flight specifically because it is operated by an A380 has become increasingly common. That brand value is difficult to quantify, but it helps airlines justify continued investment in the aircraft.

Airlines Are Investing Billions Instead Of Retiring Them

Perhaps the clearest indication that the A380 has secured a long-term future is the amount of money airlines are spending to modernize aircraft they were once expected to retire. During the pandemic, many observers assumed operators would simply return stored aircraft to service in their existing configuration before gradually phasing them out. No airline illustrates this commitment better than Emirates.

As the world's largest A380 operator, the Dubai-based carrier has invested approximately $5 billion in what it describes as the largest fleet retrofit program in its history, covering both its A380s and 777s. The program includes the installation of premium economy cabins across much of the fleet, refreshed business class cabins, redesigned interiors and upgraded first class suites on selected aircraft. By the end of 2026, Emirates expects around 110 A380s to be flying, making it by far the dominant operator of the type.

Lufthansa has also begun retrofitting its returning A380 fleet with a modern 1-2-1 business class layout, giving every passenger direct aisle access, while British Airways has upgraded many of its superjumbos with its latest Club Suite business class product. These investments are significant because they demonstrate confidence rather than necessity. Airlines rarely spend tens of millions of dollars modernizing aircraft they intend to retire within only a few years.

The A380 Has Become A Specialist Rather Than A Generalist

When Airbus launched the A380, the European manufacturer believed that rapid passenger growth, combined with increasing congestion at the world's largest airports, would drive airlines towards ever-larger aircraft capable of transporting more people between major global hubs.

That prediction was not without merit. International passenger traffic has more than doubled since the early 2000s, and airports such as London Heathrow, Dubai, and Singapore have become significantly busier. However, the shift to twin-engine aircraft ultimately limited the A380's commercial success.

Airbus originally forecast demand for well over 1,000 over the program's lifetime, but only a quarter of that number were built. Many airlines concluded that operating two smaller aircraft offered greater flexibility than flying one very large aircraft, allowing them to spread departures throughout the day and better match capacity to demand. Ironically, those same market forces have helped define the A380's long-term role.

Rather than serving every long-haul route, the aircraft has become highly specialized, excelling only where its unique characteristics offer a clear commercial advantage. Airlines no longer need hundreds of A380s spread across their networks to justify keeping the type in service. Instead, a relatively small fleet deployed on carefully selected trunk routes can continue generating attractive returns. The aircraft has evolved into a highly effective solution for a very specific set of market conditions.

Why The World's Largest Airliner Still Has A Long Future Ahead

Despite no longer being in production, the A380 is unlikely to disappear from the skies anytime soon. Around 190 aircraft remain in active commercial service during 2026, with Emirates alone accounting for well over half of the operational fleet. While some airlines, including Air France, Thai Airways and Malaysia Airlines, retired the type during or shortly after the pandemic, the remaining operators are generally those with networks best suited to its capabilities.

The pace of the aircraft's eventual retirement will depend on several factors beyond Airbus' control. The long-awaited arrival of the 777X will eventually provide airlines with a modern high-capacity twin-engine alternative, while Airbus intends to continue increasing A350 production throughout the decade. Improvements in engine efficiency, sustainable aviation fuel adoption and future aircraft designs will gradually reduce the economic case for operating four-engine aircraft. However, those transitions will take time.

For an aircraft that was once widely labeled one of commercial aviation's greatest failures, the A380 has enjoyed a remarkable reversal in fortunes. It never fulfilled Airbus' ambition of becoming the dominant aircraft connecting the world's largest hubs, nor will production ever restart. Yet success can be measured in different ways. Today, the superjumbo occupies a profitable niche that no other passenger aircraft can fully replicate, combining unmatched capacity with a premium passenger experience.
